aggregate-demand-s2.title: Three news stories from Arland
aggregate-demand-s2.html:
Arland is an invented country. In one month its newspapers report three stories:

  1. Home and stock prices in Arland jump, so households feel richer.
  2. A deep recession hits Arland's main trading partner, so foreign incomes fall.
  3. Arland's firms expect sales to boom next year and plan new factories.

Assume nothing else changes, including the price level, unless a question says so.

lras-s2.title: A year on the island of Tolva
lras-s2.html:

  3. Tolva's households, cheered by a sports victory, spend more on restaurants and travel.

fiscal-policy-s2.title: Velora's overheated economy
fiscal-policy-s2.html: Velora is an invented country. Its real GDP is 60 billion dollars above full-employment output, unemployment is below the natural rate, and prices are rising fast. Velora's MPC is 0.75. Its government wants to close the gap now rather than wait for the economy to adjust on its own.

items.q: Using the table, calculate total planned spending in Country X this year, in billions of dollars, as <math class="mac-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>C</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>I</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>G</mi><mo>+</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>M</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C + I + G + (X - M)</annotation></semantics></math>.

mistakes.why: You added imports. Imports are spending on goods made abroad, so they are subtracted: use <math class="mac-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>X</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>M</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">X - M</annotation></semantics></math>.
That is last year's total. The question asks about this year, with investment at 150 and exports at 140.

items.q: Based on the table, what is the overall effect of the two changes on Country X's aggregate demand curve?
options: It shifts left, because investment fell by more than net exports rose
It shifts right, because exports rose while imports stayed the same
It does not shift, because consumption and government spending did not change
It moves along the curve to a lower price level and less output

items.q: Which event could explain the change in investment in the table?
options: Households bought fewer new cars and appliances
Firms grew pessimistic about future sales and cut plans for new equipment
Foreign buyers bought more of Country X's goods
The government built fewer roads and bridges

items.q: Using the table, calculate Country X's net exports this year, in billions of dollars.

mistakes.why: You added imports to exports. Net exports are exports minus imports.

You subtracted the wrong way round. Net exports are exports minus imports, <math class="mac-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>X</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>M</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">X - M</annotation></semantics></math>.

items.q: How does story 1 (rising home and stock prices) affect Arland's aggregate demand?
options: AD shifts left, because households save their gains instead of spending them
There is a movement down along AD, because the price level falls
AD shifts right, because richer households increase consumption at every price level
AD does not change, because stocks are assets and not goods

items.q: How does story 2 (a recession abroad) affect Arland's aggregate demand?
options: AD shifts right, because Arland's imports become cheaper
AD shifts right, because foreign workers move to Arland
AD is unaffected, because the recession happens in another country
AD shifts left, because foreigners buy fewer of Arland's exports

items.q: Which component of Arland's aggregate demand changes first because of story 3?
options: Investment
Consumption
Government spending
Net exports

items.q: Considering all three stories together, which statements about Arland's AD are correct? Select all that apply.
options: Stories 1 and 3 each shift AD to the right
Story 2 shifts AD to the left
The overall direction of the AD shift depends on how large each change is
No story shifts AD, because the price level is unchanged
Story 2 moves Arland along its AD curve
Story 3 raises AD later, once the factories are finished

items.q: Which pair of labels belongs on the axes of an aggregate demand graph?
options: Price on the vertical axis and quantity on the horizontal axis
Price level on the vertical axis and real GDP on the horizontal axis
Inflation rate on the vertical axis and unemployment rate on the horizontal axis
Nominal GDP on the vertical axis and real GDP on the horizontal axis

items.q: The price level falls while household wealth in dollars stays the same. Through the real wealth effect, what happens?
options: Households feel poorer, so consumption falls and AD shifts left
Consumption rises, so the AD curve shifts to the right
The same savings buy more, so consumption rises and real GDP demanded rises along AD
Nothing happens, because wealth measured in dollars did not change

items.q: Put the links of the interest rate effect in order, starting from a fall in the price level.
options: The price level falls
People need less money for the same purchases, so they borrow less and lend more
Interest rates fall
Firms and households spend more on investment and big items
Real GDP demanded rises, a movement down along AD

items.q: Why does the aggregate demand curve slope down for a different reason than the demand curve for one good?
options: When the price of one good falls, buyers switch to it from other goods, and the same holds for the whole economy
A lower price level raises nominal incomes, so people buy more of everything
Aggregate demand counts government spending, which rises when prices fall
A lower price level changes real wealth, interest rates and the price of a country's goods against foreign goods

items.q: The price level in Country Z falls while prices abroad stay the same. Through the exchange rate effect, what happens to Country Z's spending?
options: Its goods become cheaper relative to foreign goods, so net exports rise along AD
Its goods become dearer relative to foreign goods, so net exports fall
Imports rise because foreign goods are now cheaper for Country Z
AD shifts right because exports are a component of AD

items.q: Firms become much more optimistic about future sales and raise their spending on new equipment. Shift the aggregate demand curve to show the effect.

slips.AD: More investment spending raises planned spending at every price level, so AD shifts right.

items.q: Nothing shifts, but the price level falls. Mark a point X on the aggregate demand curve showing the new price level and real GDP demanded.
Make it specific: build the chain from a rise in household wealth to aggregate demand.

specific.frame: Household wealth rises, so consumption ___ at every price level; ___ shifts to the ___.
specific.model: When household wealth rises, consumption increases at every price level because households feel richer, so the aggregate demand curve shifts to the right.

spending.label: Consumption
options: rises
falls

why.1: Richer households spend more, not less.

curve.label: The curve
options: aggregate demand
the demand for one good

why.1: Consumption across the whole economy is part of aggregate demand.

direction.label: Which way
options: right
left

why.1: More spending at every price level is a shift right.

items.q: The government cuts income taxes, and households keep more of each paycheck. What happens to aggregate demand?
options: It shifts left, because the government collects less money to spend
It shifts right, because take-home pay and consumption rise
It moves along the curve, because taxes are a kind of price
It shifts right, because the government buys more goods

items.q: Using the table, calculate Country Q's marginal propensity to consume (MPC).

mistakes.why: You divided total consumption by total disposable income. The MPC uses the changes: <math class="mac-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mi>C</mi></mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mtext>DI</mtext></mrow></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{\Delta C}{\Delta \text{DI}}</annotation></semantics></math>.
You divided the change in income by the change in consumption. Put the change in consumption on top.

items.q: Using the table, calculate Country Q's marginal propensity to save (MPS).

mistakes.why: You used total saving over total income. The MPS uses the changes: <math class="mac-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mi>S</mi></mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mtext>DI</mtext></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>20</mn><mn>100</mn></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{\Delta S}{\Delta \text{DI}} = \frac{20}{100}</annotation></semantics></math>.

items.q: Using the table, calculate Country Q's spending multiplier.

mistakes.why: You divided 1 by the MPC. The spending multiplier is <math class="mac-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mtext>MPC</mtext></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mtext>MPS</mtext></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{1}{1 - \text{MPC}} = \frac{1}{\text{MPS}}</annotation></semantics></math>.

That is the tax multiplier, <math class="mac-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">−</mo><mfrac><mtext>MPC</mtext><mtext>MPS</mtext></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">-\frac{\text{MPC}}{\text{MPS}}</annotation></semantics></math>. The spending multiplier is <math class="mac-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mtext>MPS</mtext></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{1}{\text{MPS}}</annotation></semantics></math>.

items.q: Using the table, if government spending in Country Q rises by 20 billion dollars and the price level does not change, by how much does real GDP rise, in billions of dollars?

mistakes.why: You divided. Going from a change in spending to its effect on real GDP, multiply by the multiplier; divide only when working back from a gap to the spending needed.

You multiplied by the MPC. Use the spending multiplier, <math class="mac-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mtext>MPS</mtext></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{1}{\text{MPS}} = 5</annotation></semantics></math>.

items.q: By how much must Brenland's government raise its spending, in billions of dollars, to close the gap?

mistakes.why: You multiplied the gap by the multiplier. Divide it: the multiplier turns the 30 of new spending into the 120 of new output.

You multiplied the gap by the MPC. Find the multiplier first (<math class="mac-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mtext>MPS</mtext></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{1}{\text{MPS}} = 4</annotation></semantics></math>), then divide the gap by it.

items.q: If Brenland instead closes the gap with a tax cut alone, by how much must it cut taxes, in billions of dollars?

mistakes.why: You used the spending multiplier (4). A tax change works through consumption, so use the tax multiplier, <math class="mac-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">−</mo><mfrac><mtext>MPC</mtext><mtext>MPS</mtext></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">−</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">-\frac{\text{MPC}}{\text{MPS}} = -3</annotation></semantics></math>.
You multiplied the gap by the tax multiplier. Divide the gap by it.

items.q: Why must Brenland's tax cut be larger than its spending increase to close the same gap?
options: Households save part of a tax cut, so the first round of new spending is smaller
A tax cut lowers the MPC, so later rounds of spending shrink
Tax cuts take longer to reach households than government purchases
The tax multiplier is larger than the spending multiplier

items.q: Which pair of actions could close Brenland's gap?
options: Cut government spending or raise taxes
Raise government spending or cut taxes
Raise government spending and raise taxes by twice as much
Cut taxes and cut government spending by the same amount

items.q: Which statement about the MPC and the MPS is correct?
options: They add up to the spending multiplier
The MPC is consumption divided by disposable income
They add up to 1
The MPS rises whenever the MPC rises

items.q: Country A has an MPC of 0.9 and Country B an MPC of 0.75. Each raises government spending by 10 billion dollars, with the price level unchanged. Which is correct?
options: Real GDP rises by 40 billion in A and by 100 billion in B
Real GDP rises by 9 billion in A and by 7.5 billion in B
Real GDP rises by 10 billion in both, because the spending is the same
Real GDP rises by 100 billion in A and by 40 billion in B

items.q: The MPC is 0.9. The government cuts taxes by 10 billion dollars and the price level does not change. By how much does real GDP rise, in billions of dollars?

mistakes.why: You used the spending multiplier (10). A tax cut is partly saved, so use the tax multiplier, <math class="mac-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">−</mo><mfrac><mtext>MPC</mtext><mtext>MPS</mtext></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">−</mo><mn>9</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">-\frac{\text{MPC}}{\text{MPS}} = -9</annotation></semantics></math>.
You divided. To find the effect of a known tax change on real GDP, multiply it by the tax multiplier.

items.q: The MPC is 0.8. The government raises its spending by 50 billion dollars and raises taxes by 50 billion dollars at the same time. With the price level unchanged, by how much does real GDP change, in billions of dollars?

mistakes.why: The two changes do not cancel. The spending is spent in full, while households would have saved part of the tax, so the spending effect (250) is larger than the tax effect (200).

You added the tax effect instead of subtracting it. A tax rise lowers consumption, so its effect is <math class="mac-m"><semantics><mrow><mn>50</mn><mo>×</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">−</mo><mn>4</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">−</mo><mn>200</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">50 \times (-4) = -200</annotation></semantics></math>.

items.q: Put the steps for finding the change in government spending that closes a recessionary gap in order.
options: Find the MPC (and the MPS = 1 - MPC)
Compute the spending multiplier, 1 / MPS
Decide the direction: a recessionary gap needs more spending
Divide the gap by the multiplier

items.q: A city gives a firm 1 million dollars to build a new stadium. Why can total spending in the economy rise by more than 1 million dollars?
options: Those who earn the million re-spend part of it, round after round
Prices rise, so each dollar of the stadium counts for more
The firm deposits the money in a bank, and the deposit counts as new spending
The government counts the stadium twice when measuring GDP

items.q: Make it specific: explain how the multiplier works for a rise in government spending.

specific.frame: Government spending rises, so incomes ___. Households spend the ___ share of the new income, which becomes ___ income for others, so real GDP rises by ___ the first change.
specific.model: Government spending rises, so incomes increase. Households spend the MPC share of the new income, which becomes more income for others, so real GDP rises by a multiple of the first change because each round is partly re-spent.

output.label: Incomes
options: rise
fall

why.1: Government purchases pay workers and firms, so incomes rise.

multiplier.label: The share spent
options: MPC
MPS

why.1: The MPS is the share saved, which leaks out of the rounds.

link.label: Next round
options: more
less

why.1: Spending by one household is income for another, so income rises again.

change.label: How much
options: a multiple of
less than

why.1: Each round adds more spending, so the total exceeds the first change.

items.q: The government raises its purchases of goods and services. Shift the aggregate demand curve to show the effect.

slips.AD: More government spending raises spending at every price level, so AD shifts right.

items.q: Based on the table, in which year did Country V's SRAS curve shift to the left compared with Year 1, because of an input price?
options: Year 2
Year 3
Year 1
No year, because the price level is not in the table

items.q: Based on the table, what happened to SRAS in Year 3 compared with Year 1?
options: It shifted left, because firms needed fewer workers
It shifted right, as output per worker rose
It did not change, because wages and oil prices were the same
The economy moved up along SRAS to a higher price level

items.q: Using the table, calculate the percent change in Country V's average nominal wage from Year 1 to Year 4.

mistakes.why: 2 is the change in dollars. The percent change divides it by the starting wage: <math class="mac-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mn>2</mn><mn>20</mn></mfrac><mo>×</mo><mn>100</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{2}{20} \times 100</annotation></semantics></math>.
You started from Year 4. Percent change is measured from the starting value, Year 1.

items.q: In Year 4 the nominal wage rose while output per worker was the same as in Year 1. What does this do to SRAS, and why?
options: It shifts right, because workers with higher pay spend more
It does not shift, because wages are not an input price
It shifts left, because the labor cost of each unit of output rose
It moves along SRAS to more output

items.q: Which event could have caused the shift shown in the graph, from SRAS1 to SRAS2?
options: A new technology that lets workers produce more each hour
A fall in household wealth that cuts consumption
A government subsidy paid to firms for each unit they produce
A sharp rise in the price of energy used by most firms

items.q: According to the graph, what does the shift mean at a price level that stays the same?
options: Firms supply less real output at that price level than before
Firms supply more real output at that price level than before
Households plan to buy less real output at that price level
Firms charge a lower price level for the same output

items.q: Which of the following could each cause the shift in the graph? Select all that apply.
options: Nominal wages rise across the economy with no gain in productivity
A new tax on each unit firms produce
Firms buy faster machines that raise output per worker
The price level rises

items.q: Why does the short-run aggregate supply curve slope upward?
options: A higher price level makes households richer, so they buy more
Sticky wages make extra output more profitable when the price level rises
Workers demand higher wages whenever output rises
A higher price level brings more workers into the country, so output rises

items.q: The price level rises by 5 percent, but workers' wage contracts will not be renegotiated for a year. What happens in the short run?
options: Firms produce less, because the price level is higher
SRAS shifts right, because firms' profits rose
Firms produce more, since prices rose but wage costs did not
Nothing changes until the wage contracts are renegotiated next year

items.q: Workers across the economy come to expect prices to rise faster next year, and they bargain for higher nominal wages now. What happens to SRAS?
options: It shifts right, because firms expect to sell at higher prices
It does not move, because nothing has happened to prices yet
The economy moves along SRAS to a higher price level
It shifts left, because firms' wage costs rise at every price level

items.q: A drought ruins harvests and raises the cost of food used by restaurants, food processors and other firms. Shift the right curve to show the effect.

key.because: a rise in the cost of an input

slips.AD: A drought raises what it costs firms to produce. That shifts SRAS, not spending (AD).

items.q: The government pays firms a subsidy for each unit of output they produce. Shift the right curve to show the effect.

key.because: a subsidy that lowers firms' costs

slips.AD: The subsidy goes to firms for producing, so it lowers costs and shifts SRAS, not AD.

items.q: Nothing shifts, but the price level rises. Mark a point X on the SRAS curve showing the new price level and real output supplied.
Which change moves an economy along its SRAS curve instead of shifting it?
options: A rise in the price level
A rise in nominal wages
A rise in productivity
A fall in the price of oil

items.q: Make it specific: explain how a fall in oil prices affects short-run aggregate supply.

specific.frame: Oil prices fall, so firms' production costs ___. At every price level firms supply ___ real output, so ___ shifts to the ___.
specific.model: Oil prices fall, so firms' production costs decrease. Because each unit is cheaper to make, firms supply more real output at every price level, so SRAS shifts to the right.

change.label: Costs
options: fall
rise

why.1: Oil is an input, so cheaper oil lowers costs.

output.label: Output supplied
options: more
less

why.1: Lower costs make more output profitable at each price level.

curve.label: The curve
options: SRAS
AD

why.1: Costs of production change supply, not planned spending.

direction.label: Which way
options: right
left

why.1: More output supplied at each price level is a shift right.

items.q: A country's government adds many new safety rules that raise firms' costs of producing each unit. What happens to SRAS?
options: It shifts right
It shifts left
It does not change, because rules are not prices
It becomes vertical

items.q: Using the table, calculate the percent change in Country L's full-employment real GDP from 2000 to 2010.

mistakes.why: 50 is the change in billions of dollars. The percent change divides it by the 2000 value: <math class="mac-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mn>50</mn><mn>500</mn></mfrac><mo>×</mo><mn>100</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{50}{500} \times 100</annotation></semantics></math>.
You divided by the 2010 value. A percent change is measured from the earlier value, 500.

items.q: Based on the table, what happened to Country L's LRAS curve between 2010 and 2020?
options: It shifted left, as the stock of machines and buildings fell
It shifted right, because the labor force stayed at 22 million
It did not shift, because the labor force did not change
It moved down, because the price level fell

items.q: Based on the table, in which ten years did Country L's LRAS shift right by the most?
options: No decade, because a vertical LRAS curve does not shift

items.q: From 2020 to 2030, how would Country L's production possibilities curve (PPC) change, and why?
options: It would shift inward, because more of the resources are used
It would not change, because a PPC shows just two goods
It would shift outward, as labor and capital grew
The economy would move from a point inside the PPC to a point on it

items.q: How does event 1 (the hurricane) affect Tolva's LRAS?
options: LRAS shifts right, because rebuilding raises spending on new factories
LRAS is unaffected, because the labor force is the same
There is a movement along LRAS to a higher price level
LRAS shifts left, as Tolva has less capital to produce with

items.q: Which event shifts Tolva's LRAS to the right?
options: Event 2, the new port
Event 1, the hurricane
Event 3, the rise in household spending
Events 1 and 3 together

items.q: Why does event 3, the rise in household spending, not shift Tolva's LRAS?
options: Household spending is too small a part of GDP to matter
Spending shifts AD; LRAS depends on resources and technology
Restaurants and travel are services, which do not count in GDP
LRAS shifts when the government acts, not when households do

items.q: Why is the long-run aggregate supply curve vertical?
options: In the long run firms are unable to raise their prices, so they stop expanding output
In the long run the economy runs out of extra workers, so firms stop hiring more
Wages and prices fully adjust, so output depends on resources, not the price level
In the long run demand for goods stops changing

items.q: The price level in an economy doubles, and over time every nominal wage and input price doubles too. What happens to real output in the long run?
options: It doubles, because prices doubled
It falls by half, because goods are twice as expensive
It rises above full employment for good
It stays at full-employment output

items.q: Which of the following would shift a country's LRAS to the right? Select all that apply.
options: More adults join the labor force
Workers become more skilled through better training
Firms build more factories and machines
Consumers become more confident and spend more
The price level rises
Firms' wage contracts expire and are renegotiated

items.q: A country adopts a new technology that lets every factory produce more with the same workers and machines. Shift the long-run aggregate supply curve to show the effect on full-employment output.

slips.AD: Technology changes what the economy can produce, not what people plan to buy, so it shifts LRAS, not AD.

items.q: An earthquake destroys many factories, roads and power lines, which raises costs now and lowers what the economy can produce at full employment. Shift every curve this changes.

key.because: the loss of factories, roads and power lines

slips.AD: The earthquake destroys productive capacity. That shifts the supply curves, not spending.

items.q: Country P makes wheat and cloth. Many skilled workers move to Country P and find jobs. Shift its production possibilities curve to show the change in what it can produce.

key.because: a rise in the labor force

items.q: How are a country's LRAS curve and its production possibilities curve (PPC) related?
options: Both show capacity: as LRAS shifts right, the PPC shifts out
When LRAS shifts right, the PPC shifts inward
